transcript.text:
This is commonly either a simple airflow/setting issue, or—if the freezer is still cold—a restriction stopping cold air reaching the fridge. A freezer-side ice build-up from a defrost fault is also common on frost-free appliances. If both sections are warm, the compressor/start side or cooling system becomes more likely. 1. Check the temperature control/display is set around 3–5°C for the fridge and -18°C for the freezer, with no holiday mode selected. A wrong setting can cause this directly.
2. Make sure food is not covering vents on the back wall or packed tightly enough to stop air circulating. Move items clear if needed.
3. Check both door seals for a gap, tear, dirt or a folded section preventing the doors closing flat.
4. Check whether the freezer is still properly cold and whether there is thick ice on its rear inner wall. This separates an airflow/defrost problem from a more general cooling fault. If there is water near the appliance, switch it off and unplug it before cleaning or moving anything. Is the freezer still cold, and is there heavy ice on the freezer’s back wall?
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
freezer still cold, about -17. yes thick white frost on the back wall, more than ive ever seen

With the freezer still around -17°C but unusually thick frost on its back wall, the most likely cause is an ice blockage from the automatic defrost system. Ice builds up behind that panel, then prevents cold air reaching the fridge compartment. A leaking freezer-door seal can also create this much frost, so it is worth checking at the same time. 1. Check the temperature setting/display is still about 3–5°C for the fridge and -18°C for the freezer, with no holiday or eco mode selected. If it is set incorrectly, correct it first. 2. Check the freezer-door seal all the way round for dirt, a tear, a gap or a folded/loose section. Clean and refit it if needed. A seal that does not close flat lets warm moist air in and creates heavy frost. 3. The useful next step is a full manual defrost: switch the appliance off at the socket and unplug it, move food to cool bags or another freezer, put towels down, and leave both doors open until all ice has melted. Do not chip at ice with a knife or use a heat gun. Dry it fully before restarting. If the fridge cools normally again after defrosting but the heavy frost returns over the following days or weeks, that points to a fault in the automatic defrost system rather than the defrost itself being a permanent repair. An engineer would then need to diagnose the defrost heater, sensor/thermostat and control side safely.
settings are 3 and -19, nobody's changed them. seals look fine, doors close ok. no burning smell or tripping. ok I can do the defrost, got somewhere to put the food for a day

The normal settings and sound door seals make an abnormal ice build-up much more likely than a simple setting or seal issue. Go ahead with the full defrost as planned. Once the ice has fully gone, dry the appliance and restart it. If there is an accessible drain hole/channel at the bottom of the fridge’s rear inner wall, gently flush it with warm water or clear it with a soft pipe cleaner—nothing sharp. A blocked drain can add to the ice problem. If the fridge recovers after defrosting but the heavy frost returns over the next days or weeks, the manual defrost has confirmed the fault area, but it is not a permanent repair. An engineer would need to test the defrost heater, sensor/thermostat and control/timer circuit; the exact failed item cannot be identified from the frost pattern alone. If it does not cool after the defrost, the fan/airflow side needs checking instead.

candidates: Airflow restriction or defrost ice build-up (medium)
Temperature setting, blocked vents, door seal or poor ventilation around the appliance (medium)
